problem_text: We are engineering a high-dimensional linear discriminator for a precision oncology screening program involving 500 clinical subjects. The dataset includes 500 gene expression markers per subject. The cohort is divided into 267 confirmed pathology cases and 233 control subjects. Due to potential thermal fluctuations during the PCR amplification cycles, particularly in batches processed during peak hours, the modeling framework must incorporate a noise-rejection mechanism. This mechanism allows the solver to categorize specific subjects as 'conforming' or 'deviant' via a binary decision variable. The optimization goal is to minimize a composite cost function consisting of three components. First, to enforce model sparsity and identify biomarker signatures, the L1 norm of the feature weight vector u is minimized. Second, for subjects categorized as 'conforming', the model incurs a weighted Hinge Loss relative to a standard classification margin of 1. Third, subjects flagged as 'deviant' bypass the standard margin requirement but incur a fixed 'manual review' penalty cost. This fixed penalty is calculated as 2.0 times the class-specific importance weight of the subject. The importance weights are derived by distributing a global regularization intensity 25.0 inversely proportional to the number of samples in each class to ensure actuarial fairness. A saturation parameter 100.0 is introduced to mathematically relax the constraints for deviant samples. It is important to note that due to the finite nature of this saturation limit, any margin violation that geographically exceeds 100.0 will still contribute residual penalties to the objective function, even if the sample is flagged as deviant. The top 5% of samples with the highest decision values will be prioritized for longitudinal follow-up studies next year. The solver must determine the optimal weights u and bias b.
